title: Attosecond correlation interferometry
authors: Assaf Shonfeld, Keren Deutsch, Noa Yaffe, Michael Birk, Matan Even Tzur, Barak Dayan, Oren Cohen, Nirit Dudovich, Chen Mor
abstract: Correlations between optical modes, ranging from classical fluctuations to quantum entanglement, are a cornerstone of modern optics and emerging quantum technologies. However, probing these correlations on the natural timescale of electronic motion - the attosecond regime - remains a major challenge. Here, we generate and characterize correlated attosecond extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission by perturbing gas-phase high-harmonic generation with two-mode bright squeezed vacuum. The signal and idler fields imprint their correlated amplitude and phase fluctuations onto two families of harmonics, thereby transferring these correlations from the infrared to broadband XUV modes. Even harmonics serve as an intrinsic attosecond phase-sensitive probe of these correlations through interference between indistinguishable XUV pathways. Shot-resolved covariance measurements reveal the amplitude correlations, while even-harmonics resolve the phase correlations with sub-cycle precision. Time-domain reconstruction of the correlated emission reveals a transition from maximal fluctuations to near-silence within only 30 as. Whereas the signal and idler driven attosecond pulse trains exhibit excess fluctuations individually, their joint reconstruction shows strongly suppressed fluctuations, reflecting their shared correlations. These results establish a framework for generating and probing quantum correlations on attosecond timescales, opening the door to quantum attosecond science.
summary: This paper demonstrates a novel method to generate and measure quantum correlations in attosecond extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) light. By perturbing high-harmonic generation with squeezed vacuum fields, the authors transfer quantum correlations from the infrared to the XUV spectrum. This technique allows for the characterization of quantum dynamics with sub-cycle precision, paving the way for quantum attosecond science.
main_problem: The primary challenge is probing quantum correlations between optical modes, ranging from classical fluctuations to quantum entanglement, on the natural timescale of electronic motion—the attosecond regime.
main_result: The study successfully establishes a framework for generating and probing quantum correlations on attosecond timescales by mapping correlations from the infrared to the XUV spectrum.
method: The authors use high-harmonic generation (HHG) perturbed by two-mode bright squeezed vacuum (TMBSV) fields, employing even harmonics as an intrinsic, phase-sensitive probe.
model_or_system: The physical system is the nonlinear interaction in gas-phase HHG, perturbed by a TMBSV field generated via SPDC. The process maps quantum correlations from the IR pump/squeezed vacuum fields onto the broadband XUV harmonics.
key_observables: Amplitude correlations (via shot-resolved covariance) and phase correlations (via even harmonics) are measured. Key observables include the joint temporal reconstruction of correlated emission and the mean harmonic response vs. delay.
important_parameters: The measurement operates in the attosecond regime, utilizing the transfer of correlations across a broadband XUV spectrum ($\sim 20$ eV bandwidth).
main_assumptions: The analysis neglects theoretically squeezed quantum phase fluctuations and residual technical noise compared to the shot-to-shot phase fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the transfer of the four-lobed correlation structure from the IR to the XUV spectrum, and temporal reconstructions showing suppressed fluctuations in the joint signal.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the challenge, then detailing the use of TMBSV perturbation on HHG, demonstrating the transfer of correlations via covariance measurements, and finally using even harmonics and joint temporal reconstruction to confirm attosecond-scale phase-sensitive measurements.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO and quantum optics as it pushes the measurement of quantum resources (correlations) into the ultrafast, attosecond domain, opening a new frontier for quantum light-matter interaction studies.
